title: The Search for Kapilavastu: Tilaurakot or Piprahwa
meta_description: Where was Kapilavastu, the Buddha's home town? The case for Tilaurakot in Nepal and Piprahwa in India, the evidence on each side and how to visit both.
summary: Kapilavastu, the Shakya town where the Buddha grew up, has two claimants: Tilaurakot in Nepal, a fortified city site 27 km west of Lumbini, and Piprahwa-Ganwaria in India, about 20 km to the south, with relic caskets and sealings naming Kapilavastu. Both have real evidence. Many scholars think they tell different chapters of one story.

sections.heading: Why Kapilavastu matters
paras: Buddhist texts say that Siddhartha Gautama was born at Lumbini while his mother was travelling, and grew up in Kapilavastu, the chief town of the Shakya clan, where his father Suddhodana was a leader. He married there, had a son, Rahula, and lived a sheltered life until, at 29, he left the town at night to search for an end to suffering. Years later, as the Buddha, he came back to teach his family.

So Kapilavastu is the setting for most of the stories pilgrims know: the four sights of old age, sickness, death and a wandering ascetic; the Great Departure on the horse Kanthaka; the return and the ordination of Rahula. The texts also tell of the town's end. Late in the Buddha's life, Vidudabha, the son of King Pasenadi of Kosala, attacked the Shakyas and destroyed their town, a story told in the Pali commentaries.

After that, the town faded. By the time the Chinese pilgrim Faxian arrived around 400 CE, he found Kapilavastu largely deserted, with a few monks and some households. Xuanzang, in the seventh century, described a ruined city with palace foundations and many stupas. Then the place dropped out of memory, and its location had to be found again in the modern era.

sections.heading: The legend of the Great Departure
paras: Buddhist tradition tells the night Siddhartha left Kapilavastu in loving detail. His son Rahula had just been born. The prince looked in on his sleeping wife Yasodhara and the baby, did not wake them, and went out to his charioteer Channa, who saddled the white horse Kanthaka. In some versions the gods muffled the horse's hooves so that no one in the palace would wake, and lifted the city gate so that it opened in silence. At the river Anoma he cut off his hair, gave his jewels to Channa and sent the horse home. The texts say Kanthaka died of grief.

Today the land around Tilaurakot is farmed by Awadhi-speaking villagers, Tharu families and a large Muslim community, and the walled mound is surrounded by wheat and rice fields. The story still shapes how the site is shown: guides point to the eastern gate as the one the prince used, and the small Samai Mai shrine inside the grove is still a working place of worship.

sections.heading: The case for Tilaurakot
paras: Tilaurakot lies in Kapilvastu district, Nepal, about 3 km north of the town of Taulihawa, on the bank of the Banganga river. It is a rectangular mound enclosed by brick fortification walls and a moat, with gateways on its sides, surrounded by mango and sal trees. The Indian archaeologist P. C. Mukherji explored it in 1899 and argued it was Kapilavastu. Later excavations, including work by Debala Mitra in the 1960s and Nepal's Department of Archaeology, exposed walls, gates and structures inside.

Since 2014, a joint project of Nepal's Department of Archaeology and Durham University, with partners and UNESCO support, has used excavation and geophysical survey to map streets, buildings and the layout of the walled town. Finds from the site include pottery types of the period around the Buddha's time, coins and terracotta, many shown at the Kapilavastu Museum next to the site.

Supporters of Tilaurakot make three main points. It is a real fortified town, the kind of settlement a clan capital would be. Its distance and direction from Lumbini fit the accounts of Faxian and Xuanzang. And the nearby Ashoka pillars at Niglihawa and Gotihawa, linked to the Buddhas Konakamana and Krakuchchhanda, match places the Chinese pilgrims described near Kapilavastu. For Nepal, Tilaurakot is Kapilavastu.

sections.heading: The case for Piprahwa and Ganwaria
paras: Piprahwa lies in Siddharthnagar district, Uttar Pradesh, India, a short distance south of the Nepal border and roughly 20 km south of Tilaurakot. In 1898 William Claxton Peppé, who managed the local estate, dug into a large brick stupa there and found stone and soapstone caskets containing bone fragments, gems and gold ornaments. One casket bore a short inscription in Brahmi that many scholars read as recording relics of the Buddha enshrined by the Shakyas, though its exact reading has long been debated.

In the 1970s the Archaeological Survey of India, under K. M. Srivastava, excavated the stupa and the monastery remains at nearby Ganwaria. They found further relic caskets in a deeper level and, crucially, terracotta sealings naming a monastery of Kapilavastu, dating to the early centuries CE. For India, this was direct written evidence: a place calling itself Kapilavastu.

Supporters of Piprahwa argue that an inscribed name outweighs distances recorded by travellers centuries after the Buddha, and that the Shakya relic stupa would stand near the Shakya town. Critics answer that the sealings show a monastery called Kapilavastu existed there several centuries after the Buddha, not necessarily that the Shakya town stood on that spot.

sections.heading: Two places, one story
paras: The debate has a national edge, and both countries promote their site to pilgrims. But many scholars take a middle view. In this reading, Tilaurakot preserves the walled town of the Shakyas where Siddhartha grew up, while Piprahwa and Ganwaria preserve the great relic stupa and a later monastery that carried the name of Kapilavastu, the wider Shakya territory. The region was one landscape long before the modern border cut through it.

There is also a caution worth knowing. Alois Anton Führer, the archaeologist involved in finding the Lumbini and Niglihawa pillars in the 1890s, was later exposed for faking finds and inscriptions elsewhere, which made later scholars careful with claims from that period. The Lumbini pillar's inscription itself is not in doubt; its text has been studied by many scholars since. But the episode is one reason both sides insist on careful excavation.

Our view, as people who guide here, is simple. Visit Tilaurakot and you stand in a town of the right age and shape in the right place. Visit Piprahwa and you stand at a stupa that held what its builders believed were the Buddha's relics. Neither visit is wasted.

sections.heading: Visiting the Kapilavastu sites
paras: From Lumbini, Tilaurakot is about an hour by road, and a full day covers it with Kudan, Gotihawa and Niglihawa. At Tilaurakot, walk the line of the walls to the eastern gate, the one tradition says Siddhartha rode through on the night he left, and sit for a while in the grove by the small shrine of Samai Mai, honoured by local villagers. Visit the museum before or after; it helps the ruins make sense.

Piprahwa can be visited from Lumbini, but it means crossing into India, which requires the right visa and a border crossing, so most of our guests see it as part of an onward journey on the Indian Buddhist circuit. If you plan to cross, check current status before you travel.
list: Kudan: stupa mounds linked by tradition to the Buddha's meeting with his father
Gotihawa: Ashoka pillar stump and stupa linked to Buddha Krakuchchhanda
Niglihawa: inscribed Ashoka pillar recording the stupa of Buddha Konakamana
Kapilavastu Museum: finds from Tilaurakot and the surrounding district

faqs.a: Kapilavastu was the chief town of the Shakya clan, where the Buddha grew up. Nepal identifies it with Tilaurakot, a fortified site near Taulihawa about 27 km west of Lumbini. India identifies it with Piprahwa and Ganwaria, about 20 km further south, where sealings naming a Kapilavastu monastery were found. Scholars continue to debate the question.

faqs.q: What is there to see at Tilaurakot?
faqs.a: Tilaurakot has excavated brick fortification walls, a moat, the remains of gateways including the eastern gate linked to the Great Departure, building foundations inside the walls, a small shrine to Samai Mai and a grove of old trees. The Kapilavastu Museum nearby shows coins, pottery and terracotta from the area. Allow about two hours.

In 1898 William Peppé excavated a stupa at Piprahwa and found caskets holding bone fragments, gems and gold, one inscribed in Brahmi with a text many read as referring to relics of the Buddha and the Shakyas. Excavations in the 1970s found more caskets and terracotta sealings naming a monastery of Kapilavastu.

faqs.q: Who first identified Tilaurakot as Kapilavastu?
faqs.a: The Indian archaeologist P. C. Mukherji explored Tilaurakot in 1899 and argued that it was Kapilavastu, partly using the descriptions left by the Chinese pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang. Later excavations by Debala Mitra in the 1960s, Nepal's Department of Archaeology and, since 2014, a joint Nepali and British team have studied the site in more detail.

faqs.q: Can I visit both Tilaurakot and Piprahwa?
faqs.a: Yes, but Piprahwa is in India, so you need a valid Indian visa and must cross the border, usually at Belahiya–Sunauli or another crossing. Most travellers visit Tilaurakot from Lumbini and Piprahwa as part of an Indian Buddhist circuit. Border and visa rules change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Tilaurakot from Lumbini?
faqs.a: About 27 km west, roughly an hour by car on rural roads through Kapilvastu district. Many visitors combine it with Kudan, Gotihawa and Niglihawa, which are all close to Taulihawa, in a single full day from Lumbini. There are simple places to eat in Taulihawa but nothing at the sites themselves.

Buddhist texts say the Shakya town was attacked and destroyed by Vidudabha, son of King Pasenadi of Kosala, late in the Buddha's life. By the time Faxian visited around 400 CE, it was mostly deserted, and Xuanzang in the seventh century described ruins. The site was then forgotten until archaeologists searched for it in the 1890s.

faqs.q: Is there a museum about Kapilavastu?
faqs.a: Yes. The Kapilavastu Museum at Tilaurakot displays objects found in the area, including coins, pottery, terracotta figures and ornaments. It is small but helps you understand the excavated walls and gates. Opening hours and entry fees change, so check current status before you travel. The Lumbini Museum also holds finds from the district.

faqs.q: Why do Nepal and India disagree about Kapilavastu?
faqs.a: Because each has genuine evidence. Tilaurakot is a fortified town in the right place by the old pilgrims' descriptions; Piprahwa has inscriptions naming Kapilavastu and a stupa with relic caskets. National pride adds weight to both claims. Many scholars now see the two as parts of one Shakya landscape divided by a modern border.
